questions.question: How do @SpringBootTest test slices work and how does Spring Boot cache test application contexts?
questions.title: Spring Boot Testing: @SpringBootTest, Slices, and Context Caching
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootTest loads the full application context and is suitable for integration tests, but it is slow. Test slice annotations like @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, and @JsonTest load only the slice of the context relevant to the test (controllers, JPA layer, JSON serialization), making them much faster. Spring Test caches ApplicationContexts across test classes that share identical configuration, so the expensive context startup only happens once per unique configuration combination in a test run.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the cost of @SpringBootTest for every test and can choose the right slice for unit-like speed with integration-like confidence.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test including repository-only or controller-only tests, causing very slow test suites, or accidentally breaking context caching by adding test-specific @MockBean in a way that creates a unique context per test class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean creates a new ApplicationContext (breaking caching) so it should be declared at the class level and shared, and mention @TestConfiguration and TestcontainersConfig as sources of shared context configuration.

sections.title: Why @SpringBootTest Makes Your Test Suite Slow and Test Slices Exist to Fix It
sections.content:
The most common Spring Boot testing mistake is using `@SpringBootTest` for everything. Every `@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context — database connections, message brokers, all auto-configurations, every bean. For a test that only checks a controller's request mapping or a repository's query, **you're paying 10–30 seconds of context startup for a test that runs in milliseconds.**

Test slices solve this by loading only the beans relevant to one layer. `@WebMvcTest` loads controllers, filters, and MVC infrastructure — no services, no repositories, no database. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories with an embedded database — no controllers, no web server. Each slice auto-configures just enough context for its layer.

But slices introduce a second problem: **context caching.** Spring's test framework caches application contexts across tests to avoid re-creating them. The cache key is the combination of configuration classes, properties, active profiles, and mock definitions. Any difference creates a new context. Understanding what breaks the cache is the difference between a test suite that runs in 2 minutes and one that takes 15.

sections.title: How Test Slices Work — The @...Test Annotations That Load Only What You Need
sections.content:
Each test slice annotation is a meta-annotation that combines `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)` with a set of `@AutoConfigure*` and `@Import*` annotations specific to one layer.

`@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads only the specified controller, its advice classes, and MVC infrastructure. **It does not scan `@Service` or `@Repository` beans** — you mock them with `@MockBean`. This is intentional: controller tests should verify HTTP behavior (status codes, response shapes, validation errors), not business logic.

`@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories, configures an embedded H2 database, and enables `@Transactional` with automatic rollback after each test. It does not load controllers or service beans. This gives you fast repository tests that verify queries, entity mappings, and constraint violations without a web server.

Other slices follow the same pattern: `@WebFluxTest` for reactive controllers, `@DataMongoTest` for MongoDB repositories, `@JsonTest` for Jackson serialization, `@RestClientTest` for `RestTemplate`/`WebClient` configurations. **Each slice is designed to test one concern in isolation**, loading the minimum beans needed for that concern.

sections.title: Context Caching — What Shares a Context, What Creates a New One, and Why @MockBean Is the Trap
sections.content:
Spring's `TestContext` framework caches application contexts using a key composed of: configuration classes, context initializers, active profiles, property sources, and **all `@MockBean` / `@SpyBean` definitions.** Two tests that differ in any of these get separate contexts.

**`@MockBean` is the silent cache killer.** Each unique combination of `@MockBean` declarations produces a different cache key. If `TestA` mocks `UserService` and `TestB` mocks `UserService` + `PaymentService`, they use different contexts — both get created and cached separately. In a large suite, this can mean 20+ context creations instead of 2.

The fix is to standardize mock definitions. Declare `@MockBean` at the class level in a shared base test class that all tests extend, or use `@TestConfiguration` to define mocks in one place. When every test in a group has the same mock signature, they share a single cached context.

Another common cache breaker is `@TestPropertySource` with different values across tests. Each unique property set creates a new context. Group tests with the same property overrides together, or use Spring profiles to standardize test configuration.

You can monitor cache behavior by setting `logging.level.org.springframework.test.context.cache=DEBUG`. This logs cache hits and misses, showing exactly which tests trigger new context creation. **If your test suite creates more than 3–4 contexts, something is wrong with your mock or property strategy.**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context — use it only for integration tests** — `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@JsonTest` load sliced contexts with only the relevant beans.
- **`@MockBean` breaks context caching** — each unique `@MockBean` configuration creates a separate `ApplicationContext`; a test class with five `@MockBean` annotations that differs by one from another class means two full context startups.
- **`@DataJpaTest` uses an embedded H2 by default** — add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` to test against the real database; requires a running database in CI.
- **`@WebMvcTest` tests the web layer only** — no `@Service` or `@Repository` beans; use `@MockBean` to replace them; tests are fast because no database or message broker is started.
- **Context caching key includes `@ActiveProfiles`, `@TestPropertySource`, and `@MockBean`** — minimize variation across test classes to maximize cache hits and reduce total test suite time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides test slice annotations that load only the beans relevant to what you are testing. Using `@SpringBootTest` for everything works but is unnecessarily slow — a repository test that starts the web layer and message brokers wastes seconds on every CI run.

**Test slices**
- `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` — loads only MVC infrastructure, the specified controller, and related `@ControllerAdvice`; no database, no service layer; use `@MockBean` for dependencies
- `@DataJpaTest` — loads only JPA/Hibernate + an embedded H2 database; no web layer; tests repository logic in isolation
- `@SpringBootTest` — loads the full `ApplicationContext`; use for end-to-end integration tests only

**Context caching**
- Spring caches `ApplicationContext` instances across test classes that share the same configuration
- `@MockBean` is the most common cache-buster — each unique set of mocked beans creates a distinct context
- Extract shared mocks into a base test class or `@TestConfiguration` class to maximize cache hits across the test suite

**Embedded vs real database**
- `@DataJpaTest` defaults to H2; if your query uses a PostgreSQL-specific function, the test passes with H2 and fails in production
- `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)` + Testcontainers runs the real database in CI — the only reliable approach for dialect-specific queries
